item.title: BRICS summit gives boost to Global South
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
BRICS summit gives boost to Global South High-quality cooperation, solidarity strengthened, foreign minister says The BRICS summit in New Delhi strengthened common ground among major Global South countries on development, cooperation, multilateralism and global governance reform amid global volatility and recurring regional conflicts, officials and analysts said as President Xi Jinping concluded a two-day visit to India on Sunday. The summit, which brought Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi together for their third consecutive year of bilateral talks, also gave fresh impetus to improving relations between the two neighbors, with broader implications for regional stability and Global South cooperation, they said. Speaking to reporters upon the conclusion of Xi's visit, Foreign Minister Wang Yi described the trip as a major diplomatic engagement with Global South countries in the opening year of China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) period. Coming after Xi's visits to Central Asia and the Middle East earlier this month, the trip was strategically significant for advancing high-quality cooperation within the expanded BRICS grouping and strengthening Global South solidarity, Wang said. In less than 24 hours in the Indian capital, Xi attended nearly 10 events, discussed development and cooperation with BRICS leaders, and held in-depth talks with Modi to chart the course of bilateral relations, Wang said. This year marks the 20th anniversary of BRICS cooperation. At the summit, Xi said solidarity and cooperation had always been the source of the grouping's strength. He called on BRICS countries to take a leading role in innovation-driven development, safeguarding peace and stability, promoting exchanges and mutual learning among civilizations, and reforming and improving global governance. At a new historical juncture, Xi had responded to the high expectations of Global South countries by reaffirming the historic mission of BRICS cooperation and charting its future course, Wang said, noting that Xi's urging elevated the strategic importance of BRICS cooperation and bolstered members' resolve and confidence to seek strength through solidarity. Speaking at a media briefing on Saturday, Sudhakar Dalela, secretary for economic relations at India's Ministry of External Affairs, said that there was a broad convergence among BRICS leaders on the need to strengthen multilateralism and to make global governance institutions more representative, inclusive, effective and responsive to today's realities. To bolster the strength of the Global South, Xi said during the summit that Global South countries should jointly defend the rule of law in international affairs, hold high the banner of multilateralism, remain committed to a people-centered development philosophy and jointly advance security governance. He proposed five initiatives for "greater BRICS" cooperation in artificial intelligence, trade and investment facilitation, digital industry, intelligent manufacturing and talent development. Lawrence Loh, director of the Centre for Governance and Sustainability at National University of Singapore's Business School, said "greater BRICS" distinguished itself through concrete plans to benefit people in countries beyond its membership. "The BRICS summit has a broader implied message for the international community — global development cannot be based on a zero-sum game mentality where development is pursued at the expense of others," he said. Swaran Singh, a former professor of international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, India, said that Xi had presented "greater BRICS" as a platform for a more multipolar, rules-based order, with a strong emphasis on practical cooperation. He said Xi's proposals overlapped significantly with India's own emphasis on technology, resilient supply chains and a stronger role for the Global South in shaping international affairs. With China set to assume BRICS' rotating presidency for the fourth time next year, Wang said the country would remain committed to, rooted in and supportive of the Global South, sharing opportunities and pursuing common development on the path toward modernization. The bilateral meeting between Xi and Modi, following their talks in the Russian city of Kazan in 2024 and Tianjin in northern China in 2025, also brought the direction of China-India relations into focus. Wang said the two leaders held candid, in-depth exchanges on strategic and long-term issues shaping bilateral relations, with their most important consensus being that China and India should be partners. Under the leaders' strategic guidance, ties have gradually emerged from a low point, with an expanding range of cooperation, record bilateral trade and more active people-to-people exchanges, Wang said. Improved relations serve the interests of the two countries' more than 2.8 billion people and are also important for strengthening Global South cooperation, he added. India's Ministry of External Affairs said in a statement on Saturday that the leaders welcomed the steady progress in relations since their Tianjin meeting and reaffirmed the need to take a strategic and long-term perspective on the bilateral ties. "Differences should not become disputes," the statement said. Wang said that each country's development offers opportunities for the other, and that China-India cooperation has significance far beyond bilateral ties, with implications for the Global South and the world as a whole. He urged both sides to build on the hard-won improvement and implement the leaders' consensus to contribute to regional and global peace and prosperity.

item.title: Mounted officers patrol Inner Mongolia's vast grasslands
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
Mounted officers patrol Inner Mongolia's vast grasslands Share - WeChat
Police vehicles are of little use across the sprawling Hulunbuir Grasslands in Inner Mongolia autonomous region, where vast stretches of sparsely populated terrain are impassable for motorized transport. Along the Morigele River in Chen Barga Banner, a unique mounted police unit takes to horseback. Officers gallop across pastures and over rugged terrain to maintain security for local herders. When nomadic families carry out seasonal pasture transfers with their livestock, the team rides alongside to offer protection and support. Guo Yuhe contributed to this story.

item.title: China's value-added industrial output up 5.2% in August
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
China's value-added industrial output up 5.2% in August China's value-added industrial output expanded 5.2 percent year-on-year in August, accelerating by 0.7 percentage point from the previous month, official data showed Tuesday, with industrial robots among the standout products. High-tech manufacturing output jumped 16.7 percent year-on-year in August, while equipment manufacturing rose 12.1 percent, outpacing overall industrial output growth by 11.5 and 6.9 percentage points, respectively, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS). At the product level, output of industrial robots jumped 34.6 percent year-on-year in August, while lithium-ion batteries and 3D printing equipment saw increases of 57.2 percent and 29.9 percent, respectively. The rapid growth comes as industrial robots are finding applications across a widening array of industries in China. Data released in July by the China Machinery Industry Federation showed that homegrown industrial robots are now used in 253 industry groups, covering more than half of all such groups nationwide. In terms of broader sectors, the value-added output of the mining sector fell 1.4 percent year-on-year, while that of the manufacturing sector grew 6.1 percent. The value-added output of the electricity, heat, gas and water production and supply sectors rose 4.9 percent. Looking at ownership, the value-added output of state-owned and state-holding enterprises grew 3 percent year-on-year, while that of private enterprises rose 3.7 percent. In the first eight months of 2026, industrial output grew 5.3 percent year-on-year, data revealed. NBS data also showed that the purchasing managers' index for China's manufacturing sector in August stood at 49.8, while the index measuring firms' expectations for production and business activity came in at 53.8, signaling continued confidence in the outlook. From January to July, total profits of China's major industrial firms reached 4.58 trillion yuan ($677.12 billion), up 17.6 percent year-on-year. Industrial output is used to measure the activity of large enterprises each with an annual main business revenue of at least 20 million yuan. Fu Linghui, an NBS spokesman, told a news conference on Tuesday that industrial production remained stable in August despite volatility in global energy and raw material markets, supported by efforts to secure energy supplies and advance the green transition. He added that emerging industries continued to gain momentum as technological and industrial innovation became more integrated, with new growth drivers contributing more than 60 percent of the increase in industrial output.

item.title: Survey finds northern China has higher obesity rates
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
Survey finds northern China has higher obesity rates A recent survey found that Beijing, Tianjin, Hebei and Shandong have the highest obesity rates in China, with approximately one in five people classified as obese. The survey, jointly conducted by Weather China and the National Center for Chronic Noncommunicable Disease Control and Prevention, ranked the country's 31 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities according to the proportion of adults aged 18 and above with obesity (BMI ≥ 28), from lowest to highest, and divided them into five levels. In contrast, Hunan, Jiangxi, Guangdong, and Qinghai, as well as the Guangxi Zhuang and Ningxia Hui autonomous regions recorded the lowest rates, with about one in 10 adults being obese on average. BMI is calculated by dividing a person's weight in kilograms by the square of their height in meters. For example, a person who weighs 70 kilograms and is 1.7 meters tall has a BMI of about 24.2. Under China's classification standards for adults, a BMI below 18.5 is considered underweight, while a BMI from 18.5 to below 24 is considered normal. A BMI from 24 to below 28 is classified as overweight, and a BMI of 28 or above is classified as obese. Overall, obesity rates tend to be higher in northern China than in the south. This disparity may reflect differences in genetics, diet, physical activity, lifestyle, and the social environment. Colder weather and longer winters may also limit outdoor activity, while traditional northern diets tend to be richer in carbohydrates and fats.

item.title: China's long past gives plenty to smile about
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
On a large pottery shard, two dots mark the eyes and a curved line forms the mouth. Just a few incised strokes sketch a tiny smiling face, resembling a 7,000-year-old emoji. It's probably part of a cooking utensil, unearthed at the Neolithic Hemudu site in Yuyao, Ningbo, East China's Zhejiang province. A sculpted pottery human head bears dot motifs on its cheeks and what is believed to be a sun symbol on its forehead, showcasing an ancient form of tattoo-like body art. With a quiet, relaxed smile, its face subtly glimmers because natural mineral mica was mixed into the pottery clay. Unearthed at the Shuangdun site in Anhui province, it's one of the Bengbu Museum's most treasured pieces. The exhibition Smile: Imprints of the Chinese Spirit in Cultural Relics brings these cultural relics together at the Liaoning Provincial Museum in Shenyang, Liaoning province, where it will run through Oct 22. Taking "smiles" as its unique lens, the exhibition explores what it presents as the spiritual core of the Chinese nation: benevolence, open-mindedness, inclusiveness, and optimism. It features more than 300 cultural relics spanning 8,000 years, encompassing pottery, jade artifacts, bronze wares, stone-carved statues, paintings, and sculptures. Curated by the Liaoning Provincial Museum, the exhibition partners with 38 cultural and museum institutions nationwide, including the National Museum of China, the Zhejiang Provincial Museum and the Henan Museum. Visitors often find themselves smiling back at these endearing relics, their own grins echoing the cheerfulness of the ancient faces, a spontaneous and cross-generational connection that needs no words. "These smile-themed exhibits bridge the gap between visitors and cultural relics. We hope museum visitors can unwind while appreciating cultural relics, finding pieces that appeal to or resonate with them, and engaging with aesthetic education and other forms of learning in a pleasant atmosphere," says Liu Yun, director of the exhibition planning department of the Liaoning Provincial Museum. She notes that many young people are drawn to trendy toys, reflecting a widespread desire for emotional value and spiritual comfort. "We need to ensure exhibitions uphold professionalism from an academic standpoint, while keeping visitors' various needs high on our agenda, such as learning about history and having spiritual resonance," she says. She adds that even if a museum visit leaves only a superficial impression, people may still recall an exhibition and proactively seek out relevant information when they encounter related topics later. "Learning is most effective when it is voluntary and self-motivated," she says. Beyond the smiles of Neolithicera ancestors, which embody reverence for life and harmony between humanity and nature, the exhibition highlights cultural relics that reflect daily life from the Han Dynasty (206 BC-AD 220) to the Song Dynasty (960-1279). Brimming with earthly warmth, these artifacts include figurines of working people and banquet performers with lively and relaxed expressions, as well as adorable pottery dogs symbolizing guardianship and household peace. A kitchen worker figurine immediately draws visitors' attention with a relaxed expression and natural smile. With its sleeves rolled up, the figurine appears poised to process ingredients such as fish on a chopping board that rests atop a water basin. Inside the basin, a tiny fish seems to leap out. The vivid scene captures the ease and quiet delight of an ordinary Eastern Han Dynasty (25-220) laborer. Another chapter of the exhibition centers on Buddhist sculptures, literati paintings and calligraphy. Among the works on display is a statue of Guanyin (Avalokitesvara) with downcast eyes and a soft, serene smile, embodying the spirit of bringing solace to all beings and peace to the world. One painting depicts a gathering of seven celebrated third-century scholars, known collectively as "the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove". Some pluck the zither and let out long, loud cries, while others raise goblets for a hearty drink. Carefree smiles play across their faces, reflecting their unrestrained spirit, genuine character and serene composure. "The smile of the Chinese people means far more than light-hearted joy. It represents an uplifting outlook on life that persists after weathering setbacks and hardships," Liu says. In the chapter devoted to mutual learning between Chinese and other civilizations along the Silk Road, various cultural relics bear witness to the route's prosperous trade and demonstrate the inclusiveness and openness of Chinese civilization. With deep-set eyes and prominent noses, the four bronze figures each hold aloft precious offerings, including a sacred vase, in dynamic poses. Foreigners presenting treasures is a classic artistic theme stemming from cross-cultural interactions along the Silk Road. The final chapter features artworks depicting contemporary subjects, including the innocent smiles of children and people from different ethnic groups singing and dancing. "From our ancestors to people of the new era, the pursuit of beauty, happiness and tranquility has never wavered ... We hope to draw on such subtle facial expressions to reflect the inner essence of the Chinese people's optimism and uplifting spirit," Liu says.

item.title: Single solution to rise of 'solo economy'
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
Single solution to rise of 'solo economy' More Chinese are choosing to live alone, reshaping spending and tourism habits Xia Xiaosen, a 39-year-old content creator from Dalian, Liaoning province, who lives alone, prefers to buy fewer items but spend more on quality goods. One of her biggest monthly household expenses is her beloved cat Statham. When she left the comfort of the family home five years ago, she soon discovered that greater independence came with a price tag. Setting up a household from scratch meant buying furniture, appliances and household items, something she had never thought about before. Living alone also changed the way she viewed money. Managing household expenses and daily chores encouraged her to budget more carefully and purchase with greater focus. Rather than buying in bulk, she now chooses smaller quantities of higher quality goods. For instance, she prefers a small box of fresh strawberries over a large bag of budget-friendly fruit. "I don't need large quantities. I prefer fresh, high-quality food that suits my pace. That is what the solo economy means to me: buying less, but better," said Xia. Smart home devices have become essential to her daily routine. A robot vacuum, a dishwasher and automated pet care tools help her manage household chores more efficiently. Her cat is central to her home life and one of her biggest expenses, costing about 400 yuan ($59.60) a month, excluding larger purchases such as an automatic litter box. But she believes the feline companionship is worth the cost. "Living with an animal shows you your own character. It reveals who you really are," she said. A growing number of young Chinese are choosing to live alone or travel independently, giving rise to the "solo economy" centered on one-person consumption. As businesses increasingly adapt products and services to individual consumers, greater autonomy and convenience have come with higher costs and everyday trade-offs. Data from China's Ministry of Civil Affairs shows that the number of marriage registrations fell from 13.47 million couples in 2013 to 6.76 million in 2025. The ministry's Civil Affairs Statistics for the first quarter of 2026 reported 1.697 million registrations, down 6.2 percent year-on-year, continuing the long-term decline. Beike Research Institute's New Era of Solo Living Report estimates that China's "solo-living population" reached 123 million in 2024 and is projected to rise to 150-200 million by 2030. Xia said a solitary life is not without challenges. When she is ill is when she feels the absence of another person most acutely, as she has to deal with everything on her own. She shares her independent lifestyle on social media, and sometimes receives hostile comments questioning why a woman would choose to live alone. "There is still a bias. Some people cannot accept that a woman living independently can feel fulfilled," she said. But living alone has expanded her social life in unexpected ways. When traveling, she often chooses hostels because they make it easier to meet new people. Her attitude toward doing things on her own has also changed. She once felt self-conscious about going to concerts or the cinema alone, but now sees those experiences as liberating. "I used to think doing things alone looked sad. Now I go to a concert by myself and end up meeting other people who came alone too. It feels free," she said.

item.title: Chinese e-bikes power worldwide shift in urban mobility
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-15
"The best thing about having an electric bike is that you just go past people," said a reviewer of DYU, an e-bike brand based in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, in an Instagram video. "Put it on high assist, and it helps with the pedaling. You can take the hills, miss all the crowds. It's a dream ride." That feeling of effortless mobility is one reason why e-bikes are reshaping urban transportation and why Chinese manufacturers are rapidly expanding overseas. China was once known as the "bicycle kingdom", when bikes were used by Chinese residents as the most common means of transportation. Today, it is becoming the world's e-bike powerhouse. Walk along the canals of Amsterdam in the Netherlands, through the streets of Munich in Germany or on the greenways of Portland, Oregon, in the United States, and bikes are hard to miss. In 2025, Chinese manufacturers exported 26.7 million electric two-wheelers worth a total of $6.829 billion. At the center of that growth was the electric bicycle — a machine that looks much like a traditional bicycle but pairs pedals with sensors, a battery and a quiet electric motor, transforming steep bridges and long commutes into manageable rides. For many riders, the appeal goes beyond convenience. Studies show that e-bikes encourage more people to cycle regularly, particularly older adults and those with limited mobility or knee pain. "This isn't just a bike with a battery," said Lu Jinlong, honorary chairman of the Jiangsu Bicycle and Electric Vehicle Association. "It's a response to how people want to live — healthier, greener and less dependent on cars." The market reflects that shift. The number of e-bike brands in the US doubled from about 100 in 2021 to roughly 200 by 2022, with most of the new entrants being Chinese companies. In Southeast Asia, rising fuel prices and worsening traffic congestion are also accelerating demand for electric two-wheelers. According to the US-based business consulting company Frost & Sullivan, Europe's e-bike market was worth 15 billion euros ($17.3 billion) in 2024 and is projected to grow to 21.2 billion euros by 2029. Globally, Fortune Business Insights expects the market to grow from $50.14 billion in 2024 to $148.7 billion by 2032. While Chinese consumers have largely embraced low-cost electric scooters for short-distance travel, European cities offer something different: extensive cycling infrastructure, government subsidies and a deeply rooted cycling culture. The region thus became an ideal testing ground for premium electric bicycles. That opportunity drew Shenzhen entrepreneur Liang Xiaoling into the European market. In 2021, Liang founded TENWAYS with a simple idea: combining China's manufacturing efficiency with European design and software-driven intelligence. Backed by investors including Hillhouse, Tencent and L Catterton, TENWAYS now sells more than 96 percent of its e-bikes to Europe and is gearing up for what could become Hong Kong's first public listing by a pure-play e-bike company. Its flagship commuter model has sold more than 50,000 units in just four years. Between 2022 and 2024, TENWAYS became the fastest-growing e-bike brand in Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg, capturing 5.9 percent of the urban commuting segment. Its e-bikes retail for between 1,299 and 4,999 euros, positioning the company firmly in the premium e-bike market. Behind that premium branding lies China's greatest competitive advantage: its manufacturing ecosystem. Industrial clusters across the Pearl River Delta and Yangtze River Delta produce nearly every major component — from frames and motors to batteries, sensors and electronic control systems — allowing companies to shorten development cycles while controlling costs. In November, Chinese e-bike maker Urtopia acquired the US heritage e-bike brand Pedego — a sign that Chinese companies are also using acquisitions to secure brand equity in Western markets. For Chinese companies, the challenge is no longer proving that Chinese brands can build premium e-bikes, but sustaining innovation in a fast-growing market where technology, design and brand recognition are becoming just as important as manufacturing scale.

item.title: US expert witnesses Xiangshan Forum's growth over 20 years
item.description:
Published: 2026-09-14
US expert's 20-year front-row seat to Beijing Xiangshan Forum's rise David Finkelstein, a Distinguished Research Fellow at the Center for Naval Analyses of the United States, shared his reflections on nearly two decades of participation in the Beijing Xiangshan Forum in a recent video posted on the forum's official X account (@XiangshanForum). Finkelstein has been a regular participant in the forum since its inception in 2006, missing only two editions. He said the Beijing Xiangshan Forum has been one of the highlights of his annual conference schedule and that he looks forward to returning to Beijing for this year's event. Over the past 20 years, Finkelstein said he has witnessed the forum grow from a small gathering of scholars into a major international event. For Finkelstein, one of the most important things he has gained from the forum is the opportunity to interact with scholars from around the world. Participants from Europe, Asia, Latin America, the Middle East and North America can gather to discuss pressing issues of the day at the forum, which gives him a valuable opportunity to reconnect with former colleagues and longtime friends in China, he said. Finkelstein said he looks forward to returning to Beijing this autumn and seeing friends from China and around the world.
